newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS: Credit Lyonnais says more aid only way out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS: Credit Lyonnais says more aid only way out.

text.p: The boss of Credit Lyonnais told French taxpayers on Friday their only hope of recouping some of the billions of francs of public money poured into the state-owned bank was by pumping in more and privatising it.

"It's in the taxpayers' interest and in the state's interest to privatise the bank in the best way possible, at the best price possible, to erase part of the bill," Jean Peyrelevade, chairman of Credit Lyonnais, said in a radio interview.

His comments came a day after the French learned that the bank, whose plight ranks as France's worst banking horror story, wanted to raid their wallets yet again. This time it is seeking recapitalisation of at least eight billion francs to prepare it for privatisation.

One newspaper, Liberation -- under the front-page headline "Should This Bank Be Saved?" -- estimated on Friday the ultimate bill to taxpayers from the bank's reckless expansion spree during the 1980s could hit 150 billion francs ($29 billion).

The bank, announcing a modest 67 million franc first-half profit, said on Thursday it would need an injection of at least eight billion francs, but banking analysts quoted Peyrelevade as suggesting on Friday that the amount needed could be more.

The recapitalisation would be on top of 3.9 billion francs of emergency state aid announced last week to repair what turned out to be overly harsh terms of a state salvage last year that would have driven the bank back into the red.

The government had no comment on the bank's recapitalisation needs. But last week it accelarated the bank's privatisation timetable from the year 2000 and warned the bank would need a third full-scale state bailout to prepare it for sale.

The latest sums, however, are small when compared with losses of at least 90 billion francs expected on sale of the bank's dud assets amassed during its expansion binge and now housed in a separate, so-called "bad bank."
Credit Lyonnais, once France's flagship bank, rocketed in size during the 1980s, then came crashing to earth in the early 1990s when property values slid and economic growth evaporated.

Peyrelevade said on Thursday the key to finding the bank a buyer was boosting its Cooke ratio, an international banking solvency standard measuring capital to liabilities, currently 4.5 percent, by at least one percentage point.
He estimated it would cost eight to nine billion francs to raise the ratio to 5.5 percent.

On Friday, analysts quoted him as saying it might be necessary to boost it by two percentage points which could involve double that sum. However, a bank spokesman said Peyrelevade was only talking in abstract figures.
Peyrelevade cast strong doubt on the government's aim of a swift privatisation, and sources close to the bank said no sale was expected until at least mid-1998.
In a privatisation plan due by the end of the year, the bank is expected to identify which assets to sell to appease the European Commission, which must approve the recapitalisation.

It must also improve weak profitability in its core French market, an uphill task in the country's depressed banking climate, where margins are among the world's lowest. Its first half banking income in France fell 5.8 percent.
Societe Generale chairman Marc Vienot, a sharp critic of previous rescues, called the saga "a dirty business" but said he believed privatisation was the only solution.

Whatever happens, it seems certain the bank will lose its independence, falling either into the hands of a foreign buyer or being taken over by a domestic rival, a humbling fate for an institution that was once the biggest bank outside Japan.
